statement.p: Find constants a and b in the function f(x)={a x^{b}\over \ln(x)} such that f(\frac{1}{4})=1 and the function has a local minimum at x=\frac{1}{4}.

static.solution:
f(x) = {ax^b\over \ln(x)}, we have f'(x) = {a b x^{b-1} \ln(x) - a x^{b-1} \over (\ln x)^2} = {a x^{b-1}\over(\ln x)^2} (b\ln(x) - 1). We want f(\frac{1}{4})=1, and since this is to be a minimum, we require f'(\frac{1}{4})=0. These conditions give
f(1/4) = {a\over 4^b \ln(1/4)} = -{a\over 4^b ln(4)} = 1 and f'(1/4) = {a (1/4)^{b-1}\over(\ln(1/4))^2} (b\ln(1/4) - 1) = 0.
Since a (1/4)^{b-1}\over(\ln(1/4))^2 is non-zero, we can divide both sides of the second equation by this term to obtain b \ln(1/4) - 1 = 0. This implies b= 1/\ln(1/4) = -1/\ln(4). Plugging b=-1/\ln(4) into the first equation gives us {a\over 4^{-1/\ln(4)} \ln(1/4)} = 1, or a = 4^{-1/\ln(4)} \ln(1/4) = {-\ln(4)\over 4^{1/\ln(4)}}. How do we know we have a minimum at x=\frac{1}{4} and not a maximum? Since f'(x) = {a x^{b-1}\over(\ln x)^2} (b\ln(x) - 1) and a \lt 0, the first term, a x^{b-1}\over(\ln x)^2, is negative. Then for x \lt \frac{1}{4} the second term is positive, while for x > \frac{1}{4} it is negative, so the derivative is negative to the left of x = \frac{1}{4} and positive to the right, and f(\frac{1}{4}) is a local minimum.
